```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 7,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(stockplotr)
```

Age and length compositions are often the most informative, and the hardest
to fit, data in a stock assessment. {stockplotr} has a set of plots for
composition data based on the figures that
[r4ss](https://github.com/r4ss/r4ss) makes for Stock Synthesis models. Each
type of plot shows the data in a different way:

| Plot | Function | What it shows |
|------|----------|---------------|
| Distributions of observations | `plot_comp(show_expected = FALSE)` | The most intuitive way to look at compositions |
| Bubble plot of observations | `plot_comp_bubble()` | Cohort strength over time |
| Distributions of observed and expected values | `plot_comp()` | An intuitive way to look at fit |
| Pearson residuals | `plot_comp_residuals()` | Blocks or stripes of misfit among years or bins |
| Sex ratios | `plot_comp_sex_ratio()` | Trends in misfit for bins with small proportions, which have small residuals |
| Mean age or length | `plot_comp_mean()` | Trends among years; Francis (2011) data weights |

Each function can plot each fleet separately or summarize all fleets. Use
`fleet` to choose fleets, and `aggregate = TRUE` in `plot_comp()` and
`plot_comp_sex_ratio()` to combine all years.

## Composition data

The plotting functions take composition data in one of several formats and
standardize it with `prepare_comp_data()`:

* A tidy data frame with columns `year`, `bin`, and `observed`, and,
  optionally, `fleet`, `sex`, `expected`, `n` (sample size), `pearson`, and
  `comp_type` ("age" or "length").
* FIMS output with `observed` and `expected` columns, such as the output of
  `FIMS::get_estimates()`.
* {stockplotr} standard output from `convert_output()` with labels such as
  `age_composition_proportion` and `age_composition_expected`.
* Output from `r4ss::SS_output()`, either the whole list or its `lendbase` or
  `agedbase` data frames.

This vignette uses `example_comp_data`, which holds simulated sex-specific age
compositions for a fishery and a survey. The observed fishery data were
simulated with dome-shaped selectivity, but the expected values assume
asymptotic selectivity. The diagnostics below should show that misfit.

```{r}
head(example_comp_data)
```

If Pearson residuals are not supplied, `prepare_comp_data()` calculates them
assuming a multinomial distribution,
$r = (o - e) / \sqrt{e (1 - e) / N}$, using the sample size `n`.

## Observations

Distributions are the most intuitive way to look at compositions. For
sex-specific data, females are shown above zero and males below.

```{r obs-dist}
plot_comp(example_comp_data, fleet = "Survey", show_expected = FALSE)
```

Bubble plots make it easier to see strong and weak year classes moving
through the population as diagonal lines.

```{r obs-bubble}
plot_comp_bubble(example_comp_data)
```

## Fits to the data

Adding the expected values to the distribution plot shows the fit to each
year.

```{r fit-dist}
plot_comp(example_comp_data, fleet = "Fishery")
```

Aggregating across years gives an overview of each fleet. Years are weighted
by their sample sizes.

```{r fit-agg, fig.height = 4}
plot_comp(example_comp_data, aggregate = TRUE)
```

### Pearson residuals

Pearson residuals are a more statistically rigorous way to look at fit.
Filled bubbles show where more fish were observed than expected, and open
bubbles where fewer were observed. Here, the fishery has consistently
negative residuals at older ages, which is the pattern caused by the
mis-specified selectivity.

```{r resid}
plot_comp_residuals(example_comp_data)
```

### Sex ratios

The proportion female in each bin, female / (female + male), can show
trends in misfit for bins with small proportions, since those bins have small
residuals. Vertical lines are Jeffreys intervals based on the sample size in
each bin.

```{r sex-ratio}
plot_comp_sex_ratio(example_comp_data, fleet = "Survey")
```

```{r sex-ratio-agg, fig.height = 4}
plot_comp_sex_ratio(example_comp_data, aggregate = TRUE)
```

### Mean age or length

The time series of mean age or length was developed as a diagnostic for the
Francis (2011) data weighting method, but it is also a useful summary of
trends in the data and the fit. Thick intervals are based on the input sample
sizes and thin, capped intervals on the sample sizes after applying the
Francis weight shown in each panel label. A weight well below one, as for the
fishery here, means the input sample sizes are too large relative to how well
the model can fit the mean of the compositions.

```{r mean, fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1) # the interval for the Francis weight is bootstrapped
plot_comp_mean(example_comp_data)
```

## Using model output

With FIMS, pass the estimates directly:

```{r fims, eval = FALSE}
estimates <- FIMS::get_estimates(fit)
plot_comp_residuals(estimates, comp_type = "age")
plot_comp_mean(estimates, comp_type = "length")
```

FIMS reports years as indices (`year_i`); add a `year` column to plot
calendar years. FIMS estimates do not currently include composition sample
sizes. Add an
`n` column, or supply Pearson residuals in a `pearson` column, to get
residuals and intervals.

With Stock Synthesis, use the output of `r4ss::SS_output()`. Pearson residuals
and adjusted sample sizes are taken from the model output, and the Francis
weights match `r4ss::SSMethod.TA1.8()`:

```{r ss3, eval = FALSE}
replist <- r4ss::SS_output("path/to/model")
plot_comp(replist, comp_type = "length", fleet = "FISHERY")
plot_comp_residuals(replist, comp_type = "age")
```

## References

Francis, R.I.C.C. (2011). Data weighting in statistical fisheries stock
assessment models. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences 68:
1124-1138.
